sentences.sentence: We re-measured seven training-free methods for action chunking in flow-matching VLAs, whose papers report numbers from desktop GPUs, on the hardware a low-cost robot runs: SmolVLA on a Jetson Orin NX.
All tests share one checkpoint and the same recorded episodes, each had its threshold committed before the run, and every number traces to a result file and a protocol commit.
On this board the vision encoder takes 151.0 of 219.0 ms of server time per chunk (25 W).
The two methods that act on the seam between chunks pass.
A gradient-free prefix overwrite cuts the boundary jump by 72 % or more, and movement-primitive seam conditioning removes most of the seam jerk.
The sampling methods do not transfer, because vla.cpp samples in sequence and every N-sample method pays for N chunks one after another.
Several training-free chunking tricks for flow-matching VLAs were published this year, with numbers from desktop and data-centre GPUs (RTX 4090, A100, H100, RTX 5090).
There a chunk costs tens of milliseconds, and spare compute can hide an extra pass.
A robot people can buy runs its policy on an edge GPU, where most of the chunk goes to the vision encoder, which these tricks do not touch.
We measured how much of each trick is left on such a board.
Our robot is an SO-101 arm [arXiv:2606.08881] with a Jetson Orin NX 16 GB.
It runs SmolVLA [arXiv:2506.01844] through vla.cpp, a C++ inference engine, on episodes recorded with LeRobot.
This paper started once SmolVLA ran on the arm through vla.cpp, when we looked at where the rest of a chunk's time went and at which published tricks could still help.
We took seven of them, each as a gate with a bar committed before the number.
Offline effects get an episode bootstrap, and latencies are medians of at least 50 calls.
The appendix maps every number to its result file and protocol commit.
We follow one chunk of ten Euler steps at full power (MAXN_SUPER), which costs 237.5 ms end to end (Fig. 1).
Vision takes 150.7 ms, prefill 14.9 ms, and each denoise step 5.3 ms.
At 25 W the server-side split is 151.0 ms of vision in 219.0 ms.
A trick that only touches the denoising loop works on at most a quarter of the chunk.
Two power modes appear in this paper because each gate's protocol froze the mode it ran in: the serving split and the boundary experiments ran at 25 W, and the latency experiments at full power.
Every number below carries its mode.
All offline effects use the same SmolVLA checkpoint and the same 20 recorded episodes, with 254 chunk boundaries per delay.
Table 1 gives every effect, bar and verdict.
Two tricks act on the seam between chunks, and both pass.
The first overwrites the new chunk's executed prefix with the actions already committed, and it passes the 50 % jump-cut bar at every delay, in PyTorch and in vla.cpp, where it adds 0.4 ms per chunk.
The second is movement-primitive chunking [arXiv:2610.39451].
Projecting each chunk onto ten Gaussian bases keeps the error within its bar and removes within-chunk jerk.
Conditioning on the last action sent removes 83–87 % of the seam jerk at +0.19° of error, against 73–84 % in its paper (we measured on the commanded stream only).
Exact real-time chunking [arXiv:2506.07339] inpaints the prefix with guidance instead of overwriting it.
It cuts the jump by less than 50 % at every delay (Fig. 2), and in PyTorch it costs 1.9× a naive chunk.
Cutting the Euler steps from ten to two [arXiv:2610.32102] saves 41 ms per chunk at full power, which is small next to the vision cost.
The paper claims that the action cloud contracts around an unchanged centroid, with a cloud ratio of 0.51 on π0.
Our ratio is 0.78, between the bar of 0.70 and the fail line of 0.85, so the claim is not proven here.
The paper also expects fewer steps to remove edge-GPU thermal throttling, and our Orin did not throttle at ten steps in either power mode.
We keep ten steps, as the protocol says while the contraction is unproven.
Two tricks sample several chunks per decision.
Speculative chunk selection [arXiv:2610.28019] samples four candidates and uses the pre-commit frame to pick the one closest to the recorded teleoperation continuation.
Offline it beats a random pick (one continuation per frame, training-set episodes, open loop).
Its paper promises no added control-step delay, but on the Orin vla.cpp samples the candidates in sequence, and a cycle costs 1,200 ms and 37 control ticks against 8 for a naive chunk (Fig. 3).
Entropy-adaptive chunk length [arXiv:2604.04161] samples 20 chunks per decision, and one decision takes 4,751 ms on the Orin against a threshold of 298 ms.
Its chosen length also sits at the floor in both task phases, and the jump is no better than with fixed chunks and the overwrite.
The prefix overwrite and the primitive projection with seam conditioning act on the seam, and each costs under a millisecond on this board.
We keep ten Euler steps until the contraction passes its threshold, since the two-step saving is small next to vision.
Exact guidance, speculative selection and adaptive length all pay for N chunks in series on a sequential engine.
If you run one of them on an edge board, check first whether your engine samples in a batch, because ours does not.
This version is offline and latency only, and the closed-loop columns on the arm, for seam smoothing and for the overwrite in the robot client, belong to a longer version.

Other chunking tricks are also reported on desktop-class GPUs, and we did not re-measure them here: extending the executing chunk instead of resampling [arXiv:2610.05719], driving reactive chunking with a latent world model [arXiv:2606.18589], and fine-tuning the policy for latency with reinforcement learning [arXiv:2608.23831].
On the engine side, TurboVLA [arXiv:2607.27205] pushes VLA throughput on a desktop GPU. vla.cpp, the engine we measure, runs VLAs on edge boards.

Two works use the same arm to evaluate policies, a standardized benchmark that reports failures and recoveries of VLA policies [arXiv:2606.08881] and a fleet of SO-101 cells that evaluates policies at scale [arXiv:2607.24481].
We re-measure the execution tricks around one policy, under bars fixed before the run.
The sampling result depends on the engine. vla.cpp samples sequentially, and we contribute to it (the overwrite runs on our fork, X).
Parity and determinism checks against PyTorch on the same board are in the gate logs, and a batched sampler would test the sampling result, but we have not run one.
Effects other than latency are offline and come from 20 recorded demonstrations of one task family (bowls), which the policy was trained on.
The arm gates for seam smoothing and for the overwrite in the robot client have not run.
We left out the adaptive-length arm gate because SmolVLA is at ceiling on this task, so a gain could not show.
Latency rows run at MAXN_SUPER and the serving and boundary rows at 25 W, which makes power mode a confound wherever the two are compared.
The study covers one policy, SmolVLA at 450M, since π0-class models do not fit on the Orin.

sentences.sentence: Every number in this paper is recomputable from the repository; this table maps each experiment to its files.
Fig. 1 — where one SmolVLA chunk's time goes on the Orin NX (vla.cpp, ten Euler steps, MAXN_SUPER): vision is most of it
Table 1: Seven tricks on one checkpoint: what each acts on, its offline effect, the pre-registered bar, the verdict and its cost on the Orin NX.
Fig. 2 — median boundary-jump cut against naive asynchronous execution (254 boundaries per delay, 25 W): the overwrite clears the 50 % bar at every delay, exact RTC guidance does not.
Fig. 3 — cost per decision on the Orin NX (log scale, MAXN_SUPER): both sampling methods miss their bar (dashed: AAC's 298 ms; PACT's bar is one chunk, 237.5 ms).
